* android-editor 130 MB
* macos-template 81 MB

* linux-editor-thread-sanitizer 330 MB
* ios-template 72 MB

This is looking at the caches here on this repo

What I mean is that if this is supposed to strip out all that doesn't change from `master` it doesn't succeed in doing so
Getting the caches down to a minimal size in itself is great though, been trying to achieve that through other means, this would be an easier solution even if it doesn't solve the "diff" part

Ahh, now I see the confusion. To clarify: stripping out changes from master isn't something this implementation does; it strips out changes from master *that aren't currently used*. That is, the output being roughly the same size as a fresh cache means it's working as expected.

With that said, further removing redundancies from the default branch is a reasonable expectation. It shouldn't be *too* hard to integrate that based on this setup. Gimme a bit to experiment some
Got it, the confusion was over the fact that it loads *both* the `master` cache *and* the specific one, not sure what the purpose for that is if it's not a matter of diffing the solutions

The idea was to make it so a rebased branch would only have to build whatever changed in the branch itself, rather than building both that *and* the redundant changes from an already rebased default branch.
Damn shame that there's no way to really test changes without just pushing it all like this. Feels like I'm working with live wire.

Will look around a bit more in detail tomorrow but the output sizes look great, and glancing at the runtime for the compilations they look correct for the equivalent of a plain re-run from existing caches, so we don't seem to be missing things, hard to stress test this indeed but it looks very promising now
I'll merge this in isolation now & start manually cleaning up some of the older caches
Looking at newly created caches it significantly strips out redundant data, would need to see that it ensures rebuild cache but shouldn't be a problem

I'll accept a short-term regression on cache rebuilds if it makes it easier to single out discrepancies. It's *already* doing that in cases like Android, where the cache is MUCH larger than it should be after a "clean" rebuild. Gonna spend a good chunk of the day following up on this
